name: Surveyor 6
intro: Surveyor 6 landed on Sinus Medii, near the middle of the Moon’s near side, to check a possible Apollo landing area. A week later it made history by firing its engines, hopping into the air and landing again. It is still standing where that hop ended.
whyLeft: Its job was finished once it proved the ground was safe for Apollo, and it never recovered from its first lunar night.
repurpose: Its old landing marks lie 2.4 m away, so a visiting robot could study how rocket blasts and 60 years of Moon weather changed the same patch of ground.
funFact: The hop let its camera look at its old landing spot from a new position, giving scientists 3-D views of the ground.

hotspots.title: The first liftoff
hotspots.text: On 17 November 1967, engineers fired these engines for 2.5 seconds. Surveyor 6 rose 3 to 4 m off the Moon and landed about 2.4 m to the west. It was the first time anything had ever taken off from the Moon.

hotspots.title: Old landing marks
hotspots.text: Scout, check the ground here: these dents are where Surveyor 6 first touched down. After the hop, its camera photographed them and saw how the engine blast had sprayed the soil around.

photo.alt: Imprints in lunar soil left by Surveyor 6’s first touchdown, sprayed by its engine blast
photo.caption: The marks from Surveyor 6’s first touchdown, after its engines blasted them during the hop.

hotspots.title: TV camera
hotspots.text: This camera sent home almost 30,000 pictures in two weeks, more than any Surveyor before it. Its panoramas showed a flat, cratered plain, a good sign for Apollo landings.

photo.alt: A black-and-white panorama of flat, cratered lunar plain taken by Surveyor 6
photo.caption: Part of a panorama Surveyor 6 took of the plain around it.
photo.licenseEvidence: Wikimedia Commons file page: licence “Public domain” (PD-USGov-NASA: work of NASA, not copyrighted in the US); figure 7-41 of NASA SP-184, Surveyor Program Results (1969)

hotspots.title: Solar panel
hotspots.text: Surveyor 6 stopped sending pictures a few hours after sunset on 24 November 1967 and was put to sleep for the two-week night. Engineers heard a brief signal on 14 December, but no useful data, and then silence.

hotspots.title: Long shadow
hotspots.text: With the Sun low in the sky, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed Surveyor 6 casting a shadow about 18 m long. Shadows make small machines easy to find from orbit.

photo.alt: Surveyor 6 seen from orbit with a long shadow
photo.caption: Surveyor 6 on Sinus Medii, photographed from orbit by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.
